newsitem.title: UK: STERLING SEEN SUBDUING U.K. JULY PRODUCER PRICES.
newsitem.headline: STERLING SEEN SUBDUING U.K. JULY PRODUCER PRICES.

text.p: U.K. July producer price data, due out at 0830 GMT on Monday, are likely to show upstream inflation pressures were still being calmed by the strength of sterling last month, analysts say.
"I expect to see another sharp fall in input prices, which will be largely a reflection of sterling's recent appreciation," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.

A Reuter poll suggests seasonally adjusted input prices of materials and fuel fell by 0.5 percent in July after a 0.8 percent drop in June. The annual unadjusted change is expected to be a fall of 8.8 percent, compared with 8.6 in June.
"I also think the output figure will confirm that inflationary pressures for manufacturers are still very subdued," Stamenkovic added.

The Reuter consensus is for a monthly rise of just 0.1 percent in output prices charged by manufacturers, after a 0.2 percent drop the previous month. Prices are expected to have risen by 1.3 percent on an annual basis, slightly faster than 1.1 percent in June.

On a core basis, excluding volatile components such as food, drink, tobacco and petroleum, there is a chance of an acceleration in the annual seasonally adjusted rate to 0.7 percent in July from 0.6 in June, even if the monthly rate stays flat.
This is because of a rare month-on-month fall in July 1996.
"This is most unlikely to signal a sustained upturn in factory gate inflation," said HSBC Markets UK economist Jonathan Loynes.

He added that the price expectations balance for the Confederation of British Industry's monthly trends survey, which is a good leading indicator of output inflation, suggests the core rate might even tick lower again later this year.
But analysts cautioned that the relative weakness of inflation pressures at the factory gate did not mean there was room for complacency about overall inflation in the economy.

Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said that if producer prices fell by one percent or half a percent it could largely be put down to the sterling effect and it was important to focus on other inflation indicators for the full picture.
"A fall does help keep inflation low, but I think what you've got to look for is where the domestically-generated inflationary pressures are coming from," he said.
"The Bank (of England) have been tightening rates for the last four months regardless of the fact that producer prices have been falling -- they've just been ignoring that to be honest."

On Thursday, the Bank of England delivered its fourth quarter-point rate rise in as many months, pushing rates up to 7.0 percent as it sought to prevent the exuberant consumer sector from pushing the economy into an unsustainable boom.
Britons have received some 35 billion stg of free shares from building societies which are turning into banks, sparking fears of a return to the spending orgy of the late 1980s.
There are now hopes of a respite from interest rate rises after the Bank said the most recent rise would bring UK rates to levels consistent with its medium-term inflation target.

As well as producer prices, next week sees a raft of UK economic data which will show whether the rampant service and consumer sectors are overheating. Retail price figures are out on Tuesday, with unemployment and average earnings on Wednesday.
The comparison between producer prices and retail prices will indicate where the dangers are.

"It will highlight the dichotomy between manufacturing and services. Manufacturing is growing at a pretty sluggish pace, being hit by the impact of sterling's recent strength and consequently inflationary pressures there are very subdued," DKB's Stamenkovic said.
But the fundamental picture is unlikely to give the markets much to worry about in terms of inflation.
"Overall I expect the inflation data this week to be good and supportive of gilts and supportive of the Bank of England leaving policy on hold for time being," Stamenkovic said.
